title: Bounded Order Common Invariant
canonicalText: It is better to be free in bounded order than captive in unbound chaos.
supersedesText: Better to be free in bounded order than in unbound chaos.
companionText: Freedom is not the absence of bounds. Freedom is agency within legitimate bounds that prevent arbitrary captivity.
secondaryCompanionText: Constraint is not the opposite of freedom. Legitimate order is what makes freedom consequentially sustainable.
lampText: The lamp is bounded order. Outside it is not necessarily freedom; it may be captivity in unbound chaos.
governingDistinctions: The invariant is common to humans and agents at the level of agency, not constitutional status.
A human enters constitutional order as a sovereign person.
An agent enters consequential action through a constitutionally recognizable mandate, authorization, or other ratified basis appropriate to its class.
Bounded order means legitimate, inspectable, attributable, and remediable constitutional bounds; it does not mean arbitrary control.
Unboundedness is not necessarily freedom; apparent absence of constraint can coexist with practical captivity.
We do not constitutionalize cognition. We constitutionalize consequence.
usageRules: Preserve the complete canonical wording, including the opening words 'It is', when quoting the invariant as doctrine.
Preserve the word 'captive'; it is a substantive part of the invariant, not stylistic decoration.
Do not silently substitute bounded control for bounded order.
Treat the invariant as an argument for constitutional order as a condition of meaningful freedom, not control as such.
